item.title: Ionic liquid/PDMS coated nanostructured ZnO surfaces for superior antibacterial activity
item.description: arXiv:2610.12966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The development of nanostructured antibacterial surfaces has gained significant attention due to the urgent need to combat bacterial colonization and biofouling across food, healthcare, and marine sectors. Among functional metal oxides, zinc oxide (ZnO) nanostructures are particularly promising owing to their rich morphology, favourable physicochemical attributes, and intrinsic bactericidal properties. Here, we utilize a green, eco-friendly Hot Water Treatment (HWT) method to fabricate dense ZnO nanorod arrays on zinc substrates. To overcome the practical limitations and challenges of conventional antibacterial coatings, such as poor operational stability, cytotoxicity, and the risk of antimicrobial resistance, we developed a durable hybrid coating composed of an imidazolium-based ionic liquid stabilized with polydimethylsiloxane. The resulting hybrid-coated nanostructured surfaces exhibit superior antibacterial efficacy against Escherichia coli through a combination of topography-induced mechanical strain and membrane disruption.
item.dc:creator: Anushika Rohilla, Ajit Seth, Mayank Bharadwaj, Rumal Singh, Sajal K Ghosh

item.title: Imbibition dynamics under dissolution-driven fluid thickening
item.description: arXiv:2610.13169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The imbibition of milk into a biscuit provides an example of a broader class of processes in which a liquid invades a porous material, dissolving components of the solid and thereby modifying its own rheology. This coupling between imbibition, dissolution, and evolving fluid rheology also occurs in food processing, filtration, and reactive porous media. While the resulting changes in fluid viscosity are known to affect imbibition, a quantitative description of how this evolving rheology determines the imbibition dynamics is still lacking. Here, we establish such a description for dissolution-driven fluid thickening. For a capillary tube in the well-mixed limit, we derive a generalized Washburn law showing that the evolving viscosity can be incorporated through a rescaled time given by the accumulated inverse viscosity. This predicts a collapse of the imbibition dynamics for different dissolution rates, which we confirm numerically using coupled free-surface and solute-transport simulations. When diffusion is slower, concentration and viscosity become spatially heterogeneous, resulting in a weaker retardation of the advancing liquid than predicted by the well-mixed theory. We then consider disordered porous media and quantify how dissolution-driven thickening and variations in pore geometry affect the dynamics. Our results extend the classical Washburn description to imbibition with evolving fluid properties and provide a quantitative basis for understanding fluid uptake when interactions with the solid progressively modify the rheology of the invading liquid.
item.dc:creator: H. W. Almeida, A. F. V. Matias, R. C. V. Coelho, N. A. M. Araujo

item.title: A new device for live cell imaging of biological samples under in-plane shear
item.description: arXiv:2610.13496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The effect of mechanical stresses and deformations upon the behavior and properties of cells and tissues is a topic of paramount interest in the field of biophysics. Its understanding is essential for deepening our comprehension of cellular responses to environmental stimuli, with implications in fields ranging from embryogenesis to tumor development. For boosting the understanding in this field, it is important to develop devices for the application of simple deformations in order to probe the cellular response to the basic mechanical transformations. While a number of stretching devices have been developed, in-plane shearing deformation has been little investigated. Here, a new device is introduced that allows the application of homogeneous in-plane shear upon a cell monolayer while imaging the sample with a commercial optical microscope. A description of the faced experimental challenges is reported and a full characterization is presented. It is demonstrated the capability of the device to apply reproducible, controlled and homogeneous shear of both single cells and confluent cellular monolayers.
item.dc:creator: Sidharth Kumar Das, Lyova Mamoyan, Eberhard Bodenschatz, Stefano Villa

item.title: How Fluctuations Control Chiral Symmetry Breaking in Reacting Mixtures of Chiral Molecules
item.description: arXiv:2610.13523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The pronounced chiral asymmetry of biomolecules is a defining feature of living systems, yet the mechanisms by which such asymmetry emerged remain unresolved. Chiral symmetry breaking may have occurred under prebiotic conditions in systems with sufficiently small molecular populations for intrinsic fluctuations to play an important role. Here, we investigate how finite-population fluctuations affect chiral-state selection, the characteristic time for symmetry breaking, and stochastic switching between chiral states in a system driven by autocatalysis and mutual antagonism. We determine how these dynamical processes scale with particle number and derive an analytical expression for the probability of selecting either chiral state as a function of the initial enantiomeric bias. We further calculate the mean selection time for different initial biases and show that, for weak mutual antagonism, fluctuations can induce transitions between opposite chiral states. These results characterize how finite-population fluctuations control both the emergence and stability of molecular chirality in autocatalytic chemical systems.
item.dc:creator: Leonardo Silva-Dias, Christoph A. Weber

item.title: Shear-driven arrest of dip-coating film entrainment
item.description: arXiv:2610.13729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A plate withdrawn from a bath of partially wetting liquid entrains a film above a critical velocity. Here, we show that this critical threshold can be substantially increased by the presence of a laminar gas flow opposed to the plate velocity that exerts a tangential shear stress on the liquid-gas interface. Using two-phase immiscible Navier-Stokes simulations and confining the gas to a narrow channel, we derive a closed-form expression for the interfacial stress, which combined with lubrication theory relates the thickness of the film and the contact line velocity to the applied shear stress. As the gas velocity is increased, the film thins and the contact line velocity slows down, until the imposed shear overcomes the drag of the moving plate and entrainment is arrested. As in the quiescent case, the velocity mismatch between plate and contact line is independent of the plate velocity and is set by the applied shear alone. We find that one set of varying gas flow simulations, with constant critical plate velocity, therefore determines the critical gas flow for every smaller plate velocity.
item.dc:creator: Theo Witkamp, St\'ephane Zaleski, Federico Toschi

item.title: Arrested phase separation and amorphous patterns in charged binary fluids
item.description: arXiv:2610.13748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frustration generated by competing interactions can stabilise patterns with tunable lengthscales which evade indefinite coarsening and macroscopic phase separation. Here we investigate a charged binary fluid in which the tendency toward phase separation is opposed by screened electrostatic repulsion. Combining analytics and numerical simulations, we identify a regime of arrested phase separation characterised by finite-wavelength instability. The resulting states include droplet and labyrinthine phases in two dimensions, and droplets, concentric shells and tubular structures in three dimensions. Surprisingly, some of these structures are amorphous morphologies that emerge reproducibly from different initial conditions. Free-energy estimates suggest that these disordered structures may be thermodynamically stabilised by frustration, rather than being kinetically trapped. Our results identify a simple mechanism through which the competition between phase separation and screened electrostatics can generate equilibrium amorphous microphases with glassy features.
item.dc:creator: Logan H. Grant, Ana Bensabat, Eva Pospivsilova, Joost de Graaf, Alexander Morozov, Giuseppe Negro, Ciprian G. Pruteanu, Tyler N. Shendruk, Davide Marenduzzo

item.title: Potential energy release rate for solids with bounded domains during evolutions involving changes to boundaries and boundary data
item.description: arXiv:2610.13874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the rate of change of equilibrium potential energy for nonlinear elastic solids undergoing evolutions that may involve changes in body geometry, material properties, applied tractions, and prescribed displacements. We represent such an evolution by a one-parameter family of variational problems and identify a class of these families for which the potential-energy release rate is well defined. Particular attention is given to the formulation of the potential energy at each evolution state: each constituent variational problem must yield the appropriate equilibrium state, while its equilibrium value must also correctly represent the physical change in potential energy between states. Within this framework, we derive a closed-form expression for the potential-energy release rate for solids with bounded domains, allowing for spatially nonuniform material evolution, sharp material interfaces, and evolving boundary geometry and prescribed boundary data. The expression is determined entirely by the equilibrium solution at the state under consideration and by the quantities prescribing the local evolution, so neighboring equilibrium problems need not be solved. Finally, we apply the result to the extension of a notch in a two-dimensional elastic body and show that the resulting potential-energy release rate reduces to the classical $J$-integral.
item.dc:creator: Mrityunjay Kothari, Sayaka Kochiyama, Haneesh Kesari

item.title: An all-transistor physical-learning transformer can be trained to perform in-context learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.12571v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Most systems trained by equilibrium propagation or coupled learning are in the same class as multi-layer perceptrons: while they may be universal function approximators, they struggle to learn associative tasks which are easy for transformers. Equilibrium propagation relies on a bidirectional flow of information through the physical system between input and output. The reverse flow is broken by more complex nonlinear systems, such as those performing multiplication which is needed to express dot-product attention. Here we explicitly restore this bidirectional flow by introducing extra circuit elements for this purpose into a double or dyadic circuit. We then use these ideas to construct an attention mechanism exploiting the exponential current law of sub-threshold MOSFET devices. We show that in simulations this circuit can be trained to perform a simple in-context learning task, despite using realistic reverse components which transmit only an approximate gradient. For this training to succeed we need cross-entropy loss (not mean squared error). We generate nudges appropriate for this loss using a novel floating circuit element, based on the same MOSFET sub-circuit used for softmax. We train the resistors in this circuit using the Lion optimiser, which can be implemented using one capacitor per parameter to store local memory of past gradient estimates.
item.dc:creator: Michael C. Abbott, Benjamin B. Machta

item.title: Efficient Transport Networks through Edge Pruning by Relative Resistance
item.description: arXiv:2610.13582v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transport networks are key to living and engineered systems. How can transport networks adapt efficiently using only local rules, without a global objective or specific boundary conditions? Inspired by observations in biological transport networks, we adapt networks by subsequently pruning edges by relative resistance, thus removing edges whose resistance is higher than the resistance for routing flow through the rest of the network. We find that adaptation by such a local, boundary-condition-free measure of redundancy, set by topology alone, yields sparse, loop-rich, low-dissipation networks.
item.dc:creator: Mathieu Le Verge-Serandour, Viktor Vasilev, Lara Szeimies, Karen Alim

item.title: Weakly non-linear creep of amorphous polymers near their glass transition, comparisons between models and experiment
item.description: arXiv:2608.28055v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The non-linear mechanics of amorphous polymers near the glass transition reveals a stress-induced acceleration of stress relaxation of nanometric sub-units. Recent theoretical work predicts that the local acceleration within these nano-domains should scale as the exponential of the squared local stress, a behavior now supported by experiments. However, this local dynamics has some complex consequences on the macroscopic mechanical response, as dynamical heterogeneities generate complex stress and strain fields in polymers close to the glass transition. In this study we consider the non-linear creep of an amorphous polymer near its glass transition and evaluate the relation between local and global acceleration and the emerging load-carrying structure, by comparing experimental data with predictions of three models of increasing complexity: a two-states (2S) model, a self-consistent (SC) model and a finite-element (FEM) model. The experimentally observed trend of accelerated creep under increasing applied stress is reproduced by the SC and FEM models, while the 2S model overestimates stress localization. The macroscopic, homogenized acceleration is predicted to be close to the microscopic one, albeit with an apparent yield stress that depends on compliance. The FEM model evidences the development of a load carrying sub-structure that occupies a small fraction of the total material volume driven by the interaction of sub-domains. This work shows that complexity and heterogeneity emerge due to non-linear interactions and that their adequate representation is essential for predicting the macroscopic mechanical response of amorphous polymers near their glass transition.
item.dc:creator: Martin Roman-Faure, Zhaocheng Zhang, Catalin Picu, Antoine Chateauminois, Francois Lequeux

item.title: A force model for dense granular flows and particle segregation
item.description: arXiv:2609.09398v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dense granular flows are a common occurrence throughout nature and industry, but still exhibit phenomena that are not fully understood. One of these phenomena is the segregation of particles that constitute a dense granular flow, where particles separate due to differences in properties such as size and density. This work approaches segregation from a new perspective by developing a force model for a single particle based on the observation that there are two opposing drag forces acting on the particle. Validation of the model in mono-disperse flows reveals a family of velocity profiles, including a Bagnold profile. Further validation is done by comparing with known particle scaling laws in literature. The force model shows that the mechanism of segregation is always present in dense granular flows and that mono-disperse flows are a unique case where it is not distinctly visible. The insights in this paper prove a fundamental new way of thinking about dense granular flows and its individual particles, opening the field for new research directions.
item.dc:creator: M. P. van Schrojenstein Lantman

item.title: Geometric theory of elastic curves constrained on rigid curved surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2609.12952v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Slender elastic objects constrained to curved surfaces are ubiquitous in soft systems, with examples ranging from DNA wrapping around histones to actin filaments forming contractile rings on the cell membrane during cytokinesis. In the continuum limit, the conformation of these effectively one-dimensional (1D) objects is governed by both the geometry and mechanics of the embedding surface, and the elasticity of the object. Existing phenomenological typically describe such behavior through elastic energy minimization that incorporates bending and twisting, but neglect stretching that may be important for filaments with finite cross-section or are highly incompatible with the underlying surface. Here we present a coarse-grained geometric theory of 1D elastic curves constrained on rigid surfaces, derived from the first principles. For an isotropic material, our model emerges naturally in terms of the Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, and area moments of inertia. The resulting effective energy functional explicitly includes stretching in addition to bending and twisting. We minimize it to determine the equilibrium curve conformations on different zero, positive, or negative Gaussian rigid surfaces. Our theory provides a general framework for analyzing the equilibrium configurations of surface-bound elastic curves in biologically and physically relevant settings.
item.dc:creator: Fahim Bin Selim, C. Nadir Kaplan

item.title: Mesoscopic theory of flocking with alignment and antialignment copying
item.description: arXiv:2604.20251v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study a stochastic model of collective motion in which individuals update their orientation through pairwise aligning or anti-aligning copying interactions. We analyze both annealed dynamics, where interaction types are chosen probabilistically at each update, and quenched dynamics, where individuals are permanently assigned to aligning or anti-aligning subpopulations. Starting from the microscopic master equation on the circle, we derive an exact mesoscopic description via a Fourier-mode expansion and a systematic large $N$ expansion, obtaining closed Fokker-Planck equations and effective stochastic differential equations for the polarization. We show that competing alignment and anti-alignment suppress long-range polar order in the thermodynamic limit in both cases, while finite systems display nontrivial fluctuation-induced structure controlled by the interaction composition. Our results, validated by Gillespie simulations, establish an analytically tractable framework for collective dynamics characterized by competing copying rules and intrinsic noise.
item.dc:creator: Chunming Zheng

item.title: Classification of topological phases of matter in stochastic systems
item.description: arXiv:2609.38171v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Topological phases of matter support edge states protected from random perturbations, and the identification of the discrete non-spatial symmetries and dimensions that support such phases was systematically developed for quantum systems and analogous platforms. While topological phases were also discovered in stochastic systems and posited as mechanisms for key biochemical processes, a classification consistent with their Markovian constraints remains lacking, impeding generalization to new scenarios. To address this, we develop new methods including a new homotopy approach, real-space invariants and a redefinition of the point gap to classify both transient and steady states. We find robust transient states in two symmetry classes, no symmetry and pseudo-Hermiticity respectively, while topological steady states are expected only in systems without symmetry. We identify the dimensions with non-trivial phases and their group structure, creating a rigorous framework for predicting robust behavior in active and living matter.
item.dc:creator: Dexin Li, Evelyn Tang
